strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies inference-time efficiency (number of retrieval searches) as an under-studied metric in multi-hop RAG, complementing the current focus on accuracy-only reporting.

Useful and somewhat surprising empirical finding that an optimized few-shot ReAct baseline (tens of examples) matches or exceeds heavily fine-tuned methods like LeReT and Search-R1 on recall/EM, which is a valuable calibration for the field.

The two-stage design (SFT for exploration/coverage, RL/GRPO for learning when to stop) is sensible, and the ablation against FRUGALRAG-SFT and FRUGALRAG-Explore reasonably isolates the contribution of the RL stage.

Broad evaluation: three standard multi-hop benchmarks, three base models (3B/7B/8B), multiple metrics (F1/EM/Match, Recall, Support-F1, search latency), plus a matched-retriever comparison against CoRAG (E5 + KILT) that improves comparability.
Training data efficiency claim (1000 examples vs. 100K+) is supported, and the appendix provides enough training detail (GRPO settings, reward ranges, hardware) for reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: adaptive retrieval budgets and RL for retrieval decisions are explored in prior work (e.g., Adaptive-RAG, Search-R1, LeReT, IRCoT variants), and the core contribution — SFT for query generation plus RL for a stopping decision — is an incremental recombination rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Efficiency is measured only as the number of searches; token-level cost, prompt length growth with context, and wall-clock latency are not reported. Since FRUGALRAG-Explore accumulates long contexts, the true cost tradeoff (and whether Stage-2 halving of searches translates to proportional latency reduction) is not fully established.

Comparisons to Search-R1/LeReT/CoRAG remain partially apples-to-oranges (different retrievers, indices, model sizes, and answer generators), and the paper itself acknowledges metric overlap issues; several headline comparisons rely on subsets of metrics.

The reward design is complex and somewhat underspecified: the definition of the optimal rollout length h* is tied to a reference policy's recall behavior (circularity risk), and sensitivity to threshold τ, Rmax, and α is not analyzed.

Signs of rushed writing and possible copy errors: broken reference (Table ?? on p.4), 'Qwen3.5' typos, duplicated 'we note that we note that', and identical CoT+RAG rows across all three models in Tables 1-2 that look suspicious.

No variance/significance reporting or multiple seeds, so gains of ~1-3 F1 points over ReAct FS in some settings are hard to judge; the MuSiQue gains over ReAct FS (18.71 vs 18.84) are within noise yet framed favorably.

The 'small training cost' claim omits that Stage 1 uses oracle selection against ground-truth documents (best-of-n by recall), which is a privileged signal not available in all real settings; the limitation is only implicitly addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and practically important angle: inference-time efficiency (number of retrieval searches) in multi-hop RAG, rather than only accuracy.

The demonstration that a well-prompted ReAct baseline (ReAct FS) matches or beats heavily fine-tuned methods (LeReT, Search-R1) is a valuable and honest finding for the community, and supports the central claim that large-scale fine-tuning is not necessary for good RAG metrics.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: three standard multi-hop benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue), three model scales (3B/7B/8B), both retrieval-level and answer-level metrics, and an additional comparison against CoRAG under a replicated E5/KILT setup.

The two-stage decomposition (SFT for exploration/coverage, RL only for learning when to stop) is a sensible design, and the ablations (FRUGALRAG-SFT vs FRUGALRAG vs FRUGALRAG-Explore, adaptive vs fixed-budget analysis in Fig. 1) directly probe the claimed contribution.

Training data efficiency (1000 examples vs 100K+) is a meaningful practical advantage, and the appendix provides enough hyperparameter and implementation detail (TRL, DSPy, GRPO settings, index construction) to make reproduction plausible, with a codebase attached for review.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially SFT on oracle-selected ReAct rollouts followed by GRPO with a stopping-penalty reward. Each ingredient (ReAct rollouts, DSPy prompt bootstrapping, GRPO, recall-based rewards) is existing, and the combination, while reasonable, is not a deep technical contribution.

The reward design depends on an oracle-optimal stopping point h* computed against ground-truth documents, and dataset generation selects rollouts by recall against ground truth. This makes the 'frugality' signal privileged at training time, and the paper does not discuss how sensitive the method is to this or how it would behave when gold evidence is noisy or unavailable.

The headline 'nearly half the cost' claim is mostly driven by HotPotQA; on 2Wiki and MuSiQue the search reduction is much smaller (-19.87%, -21.17%), and Table 3 even shows recall *decreases* vs FRUGALRAG-Explore on 2Wiki and MuSiQue under ColBERT. The abstract overstates the generality of the efficiency gains.

Baseline comparisons are uneven and not always apples-to-apples: many cells for Search-R1 and LeReT are '-' due to differing model sizes and retrievers, and the comparison uses 'overlapping subsets of metrics.' The claim of outperforming state-of-the-art is therefore weaker than presented; a controlled head-to-head under a single retriever/index is largely missing.

The RL contribution is undercut by the authors' own ablation: FRUGALRAG-SFT is comparable to full FRUGALRAG with Qwen2.5-7B, suggesting Stage 2 may be unnecessary at larger scales; no statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported for any comparison.

The paper is not polished: a broken cross-reference ('Table ??'), duplicated phrasing ('we note that we note that'), typos ('Qwen3.5-3B-Instruct', 'logit produce', 'when to sufficient evidence has been gathered'), inconsistent naming (CoT+RAG rows identical across models suggest copy-paste errors), and low absolute answer metrics on MuSiQue that are not analyzed.

Analysis has gaps: the 'optimal searches' histogram (Fig. 1a) is derived from FRUGALRAG-Explore's own trajectories, which partially circularizes the adaptive-budget argument; latency is measured only as number of searches, ignoring token/context-length costs that grow with each hop, which matters for the claimed real-world latency benefit.

strengths: Clear and compelling problem framing: the paper identifies inference-time efficiency (number of retrieval searches) as an underexplored metric in multi-hop RAG, complementing the usual accuracy/recall focus, and this framing is well-motivated in the introduction and related work.

The finding that a well-optimized ReAct few-shot baseline (using only tens of examples) matches or exceeds recent heavily fine-tuned methods (LeReT, Search-R1) on several metrics is a valuable, actionable insight for the community and is well supported by Table 1 and Table 2.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three standard multi-hop benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue), three base models (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Llama3.1-8B), multiple metric families (answer F1/EM/Match, Recall, Support-F1, search count), and comparisons against prompting baselines, SFT/RL fine-tuned baselines (Search-R1, LeReT), and test-time scaling (CoRAG).

The CoRAG comparison (Table 3) is done carefully: the authors replicate the CoRAG retrieval setup (E5-large, KILT index) and use publicly released CoRAG outputs rather than comparing across incompatible setups, which strengthens the claims.

The two-stage design (SFT for exploration/recall, GRPO for learning when to stop) is clearly motivated with the observation that joint optimization is unstable, and the ablation with FRUGALRAG-SFT supports the claim that RL specifically helps with stopping/efficiency.

Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters (learning rates, batch sizes, GPU setup, GRPO group size, KL penalty), a full algorithm pseudocode, dataset/index construction details in the appendix, and code promised to be released.
Honest limitations section covering generalization to new domains, data scaling, and joint training of generator and decomposer.
weaknesses: The definition of the optimal stopping point h* is somewhat circular: it is derived using FRUGALRAG-Explore itself as the reference policy for maximum achievable recall within budget B, meaning the reward and the claimed 'optimal' stopping are defined relative to the method's own Stage-1 policy rather than an independent notion of question difficulty or answer sufficiency.

The 'Latency' metric counts only the number of search operations; it ignores token-level generation cost, wall-clock time, and the fact that FRUGALRAG's prompts accumulate documents across hops (longer prompts). The efficiency story would be stronger with wall-clock or token-based measurements. Similarly, the '% Tradeoff' metric (average performance per search) is a somewhat ad hoc aggregate whose weighting of F1/EM/Match is arbitrary.

Cross-method comparability remains limited despite the acknowledged caveats: Search-R1 and CoRAG use different retrievers/indices and jointly trained answer generators, and several table cells are missing ('-'). Some headline claims (e.g., outperforming Search-R1 on EM 'in 2 out of 3 datasets') rest on these non-equivalent comparisons, and on 2Wiki the method trails Search-R1 (36.13 vs 41.40 EM for Qwen2.5-7B).

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues reduce confidence: the text refers to 'Qwen3.5-3B/7B-Instruct' in Section 4.3 (apparently typos); a MuSiQue claim states F1 18.71 'slightly improving over ReAct's 18.84' which is contradictory; there is a dangling reference 'Table ??' on page 4; and Table 2 for Llama3.1-8B Naive appears to have a shifted/missing cell (EM missing).

The reward function (Eq. 1) is complex and the log((1-Δ)/Δ) form is not derived or justified; sensitivity to the hyperparameters R_max, α, and τ is not analyzed, which weakens claims of robustness of the RL stage.

Results are somewhat mixed for FRUGALRAG vs FRUGALRAG-Explore: Explore achieves the best recall/Support-F1 on most settings while FRUGALRAG sometimes trades off both recall and answer quality (e.g., MuSiQue with Llama3.1-8B drops F1 from 23.44 to 21.23 and recall from 37.11 to 33.90), so the headline 'competitive metrics at nearly half the cost' does not hold uniformly across datasets and models.

Novelty is moderate: the components (ReAct-style rollouts, SFT on filtered rollouts, GRPO) are established techniques; the main contribution is the two-stage decomposition and the efficiency-focused framing rather than a fundamentally new method. The scope is limited to multi-hop QA over Wikipedia-like corpora, and generalization (e.g., to open-domain search engines or other domains) is untested.

Only a single epoch of SFT and a fixed 400-step GRPO run are reported; no analysis of training stability, checkpoint sensitivity, or variance across seeds, which is important given the paper's own claim that single-stage optimization is unstable.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing: the paper argues RL's role in multi-hop RAG should be to optimize (reduce) test-time search rather than scale it up, supported by the observation that a well-prompted ReAct baseline already achieves high recall (79.6% on HotPotQA), which strengthens the experimental credibility of the claim.

Comprehensive evaluation: three multi-hop benchmarks (HotPotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue) under a common FlashRAG/E5 backend, three retrievers (E5, ColBERTv2, Qwen3-8B), 14+ baselines including recent RL-based methods (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, CoRAG, O2-Searcher, SimpleDeepSearcher), and zero-shot transfer to BrowseCompPlus.

Extensive ablations: effect of Stage-1 SFT, alternative reward formulations, heuristic stopping rules (fixed-depth baselines), sample-count scaling (100-5000), base-model swap (Llama3.1-8B), RL training stability across three seeds, token/FLOPs/latency efficiency tables, and budget sensitivity analysis.

Interesting design insight: decoupling 'exploration' (SFT to maximize evidence coverage, including rollouts without FINISH) from 'learning to stop' (RL with a stopping-time reward), with empirical evidence that single-stage joint optimization is unstable and that Stage-2 roughly halves searches while improving MBE.

Data efficiency is a practically meaningful contribution: competitive results with 1,000 examples vs. 100k+ for CoRAG/Search-R1, plus modular decoupling of the reasoner from an off-the-shelf answer generator.

Adaptive compute behavior is convincingly demonstrated: strong correlation between question difficulty (ground-truth hops/evidence count) and number of issued queries (r=0.82/0.95), plus qualitative traces.
weaknesses: The headline 'state-of-the-art' claims require qualification: CoRAG achieves higher MBE on 2Wiki (59.0 vs 50.9-51.2) and MuSiQue (40.5 vs 39.9), and higher recall on 2Wiki (65.4 vs 58.8); R1-Searcher achieves higher recall on MuSiQue (57.7 vs 53.3). FrugalRAG's advantage is primarily on the efficiency trade-off and data efficiency, not absolute accuracy.

The Efficiency Tradeoff metric (MBE+Recall)/(2×Searches) is ad hoc and linear in searches with an arbitrary scaling; it inflates the appearance of superiority. Table 10-12 show FrugalRAG actually has the highest token counts and highest latency among the compared 7-8B methods (e.g., 0.24s vs 0.065s for Search-R1 on HotPotQA), which partially undercuts the 'frugal' framing beyond search-call counting.

Training requires ground-truth evidence documents Y (used for recall-based data selection, reward, h*, and τ). The claim of avoiding answer supervision is somewhat overstated—gold evidence annotations are arguably as hard to obtain as answers in real domains, and the reward depends on h* and τ derived from a reference policy (FrugalRAG-Explore), introducing circularity and unexamined sensitivity.

Moderate novelty: two-stage SFT-then-RL with a stopping reward is a sensible but incremental combination of existing ideas (ReAct-style rollouts, DSPy bootstrapping, GRPO); Adaptive-RAG and related work already target difficulty-adaptive retrieval, and the main novelty is the specific reward shaping and data-efficiency demonstration.

Cross-paper baseline comparability is imperfect: several baseline numbers are reported from different settings/retrievers, and self-RAG 13B shows identical MBE/recall to 7B, suggesting some rows may be taken from prior reports rather than re-run.

Some inconsistencies and clarity gaps: recall values differ between Table 1 (82.80 ColBERTv2) and Table 2 context; the reward function's piecewise definition (late-stop penalty cap, ∆ clipping) and the 90/10 FINISH sampling mix are under-justified; code is only 'planned' for release, limiting reproducibility.

BrowseCompPlus zero-shot result (20-21%) is below frontier models (Sonnet 4 at 37%) and the search budget generalization claim is trained-on-6/evaluated-at-7-10, which is interesting but the framing in the abstract slightly overstates the strength of this result.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored angle: using RL to reduce retrieval compute (learn when to stop) rather than to scale up reasoning, which is a sensible reframing of RL for RAG.

The evaluation is broad: 14 baselines, three multi-hop benchmarks, three retrievers, multiple answer generators, cross-dataset generalization, RL training stability over three seeds, and comparison against fixed-depth heuristic stopping rules in the appendix.

The paper is commendably honest in several places, e.g., acknowledging that a simple ReAct+DSPy baseline achieves higher recall (79.6%) than RL methods like LeReT, and that FRUGALRAG-Explore degrades recall relative to the explore policy.

The adaptive behavior analysis (Table 4, correlations of query count with question difficulty) and the efficiency ablations (Tables 7-9) provide useful evidence that the model scales search with difficulty.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core method is a fairly standard combination: ReAct-style SFT on self-generated (oracle-filtered) trajectories followed by GRPO with a stopping-dependent reward. Adaptive retrieval depth has been studied extensively (Adaptive-RAG, DRAGIN, Self-RAG), and RL for search tool-calling is well covered (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, LeReT). The two-stage decomposition is a reasonable engineering contribution but not a conceptual advance.

The central claim—that RL learns 'when to stop' in a way heuristics cannot—is weakened by the paper's own appendix. On HotPotQA, Heuristic 1 using FRUGALRAG-Explore achieves 70.9 recall with 3 searches vs. 70.4 with 2.89 for the learned policy (Table 9); the gains from RL over a simple calibrated fixed depth are marginal. The adaptive-stopping story is only convincingly supported on 2Wiki/MuSiQue.

The 'frugal'/efficiency narrative is contradicted by the paper's own efficiency tables (10-12): FRUGALRAG has the highest average tokens (9,138-11,914) and the highest latency (0.24-0.47s) among all compared 7B methods, and lower recall than R1-Searcher on MuSiQue (52.6 vs 57.7). The 'Efficiency Tradeoff' metric, (MBE+Recall)/(2*Searches), is ad hoc and artificially privileges the method's operating point; no justification is given for this functional form.

The 1000-example claim is oversold. Stage 1 dataset generation is oracle-guided: at every hop, the best-of-n trajectory is selected by recall against gold evidence documents, requiring expensive rollout computation, DSPy prompt bootstrapping, and ground-truth evidence annotations. The framing that the method needs 'no answer annotations' is misleading—gold evidence documents are themselves a strong form of supervision that may be as hard to obtain as answers in real domains, which the paper itself identifies as a motivation.

The BrowseCompPlus result is framed as surpassing DeepSeek-R1 and Search-R1-32B, but 20-21% accuracy is well below frontier commercial models (Sonnet 4: 37.35%) and only modestly above non-agentic baselines. Claiming SOTA on this benchmark is not supported; the comparisons to much larger models feel like framing rather than a substantive win.

Evaluation reliability concerns: the primary answer metric is an LLM judge (Qwen3-32B), with no reported human validation or agreement analysis. The recall metric is defined as 'ground truth answer present in retrieved documents' (answer-string recall), which conflates answer surface matching with evidence retrieval and may be gamed by trivially matching question tokens; document-level metrics are deferred to the appendix where FRUGALRAG's precision/F1 on 2Wiki (15.45) is actually worse than several baselines.

Some inconsistencies and clarity issues: 2Wiki recall is reported as 58.80/59.90/60.40 in different tables without explanation; the abstract's 'cutting retrieval cost nearly in half' only holds relative to their own Explore stage, not against baselines (CoRAG uses 4 searches vs. FRUGALRAG's 2.89); the reward function and h* computation depend on the reference policy's performance, making the setup circular and sensitivity to tau unexplored.

Reproducibility: code is only 'planned to be released,' and the oracle-driven data generation procedure has many unspecified degrees of freedom (n bootstrap prompts, hop budget, seed questions), making exact replication difficult.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated thesis: RL should be used to *reduce* test-time retrieval rather than scale it up, reframing the goal from accuracy gains to efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. This is a useful perspective for the RAG/RL literature.

The two-stage design (SFT 'explore' policy followed by GRPO-based stopping optimization) is well described, and the reward design (Eq. 1) that penalizes both late and early stopping relative to h* is sensible and clearly specified.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this area: 14 baselines under a common retriever backend (Table 2), three retrievers, multiple answer generators, base-model ablation (Llama3.1-8B, Table 6), reward-design ablations (Table 8), Stage-1 necessity ablation (Table 7), comparison against fixed heuristic stopping rules (Table 9), token/FLOP/latency efficiency tables (Tables 10-12), retrieval precision/F1 (Table 13), cross-dataset generalization (Table 14), and RL run stability (Appendix D).
Notable data-efficiency result: competitive performance with only 1,000 training examples versus 100k+ for prior RL/RAG methods, with a sample-count ablation supporting the low-data claim.

Zero-shot transfer to BrowseCompPlus (Table 3) with adaptively increased query counts is a convincing out-of-distribution result relative to open SLM baselines, and the difficulty-correlation analysis (r=0.82/0.95, Table 4) supports the 'adaptive' claim.
Strong emphasis on building and honestly reporting competitive prompting baselines (ReAct+DsPy beating fine-tuned methods on recall), which strengthens the credibility of the comparisons.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the method is a fairly standard combination of best-of-n rollout SFT plus GRPO with a hand-crafted stopping reward; adaptive retrieval depth has been explored (Adaptive-RAG, DRAGIN, CoRAG variants), so the contribution is primarily an empirical recipe rather than a new technique.

The stopping reward is defined via evidence recall (c >= tau) rather than answer correctness, and tau is calibrated against the Stage-1 Explore policy's own performance, introducing potential circularity: the model may learn to stop when *recall-like* evidence is present without a principled link to answerability; the answer-level gains may partly be a side effect.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence: (a) on BrowseCompPlus, frontier closed models (Sonnet 4 / Opus 4 at ~37%) substantially outperform the reported ~20-21% accuracy, so 'surpasses SLM-based and other baselines' should be qualified; (b) Table 9 shows Heuristic 1 with the Explore policy achieves *higher* recall on HotPotQA (70.9 vs 70.4) with comparable searches, which sits awkwardly with the claim that fixed-depth heuristics 'consistently underperform'.

Metric inconsistencies across tables (e.g., FrugalRAG 2Wiki recall 58.8 in Table 2 vs 59.9 in Table 13; MuSiQue 53.3 vs 52.6; MBE differences between Table 1 and Table 2 for the same model) are unexplained and erode confidence in the reported numbers; the recall metric itself (answer string present in retrieved docs) is a weak proxy for evidence quality, and precision/F1 results (Table 13) actually show FrugalRAG behind CoRAG on 2Wiki and MuSiQue.

FRUGALRAG is not the best method on accuracy: CoRAG achieves top MBE on 2Wiki and MuSiQue with much lower variance across datasets, so the headline contribution rests mainly on the efficiency axis and data efficiency, and the ad-hoc Efficiency Tradeoff metric ((MBE+Recall)/(2*Searches)) is not a validated or universally accepted measure.

Latency in Table 10-12 is actually worse than several baselines (0.24-0.47s vs 0.06-0.15s), which complicates the 'efficiency' narrative; only search counts clearly favor the method, and the paper's argument that token/tool-call cost dominates is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is only 'planned to be released', and Stage-1 depends on sensitive few-shot prompt bootstrapping and dataset generation choices; the 1000-example claim also relies on ground-truth documents (not answers) for rollout selection, which may not be as available in realistic domain-adaptation settings as the paper implies.
Evaluation is on development splits of the training benchmarks (following FlashRAG protocol), so 'state-of-the-art' claims are effectively on dev sets rather than held-out test sets.
